To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

differential stimuli can have stimulus control functions in the absence of differential reinforcement, and that the stimulus control functions of differential stimuli are not necessarily independent of the reinforcement contingencies that are associated with them.
the differential stimulus effects on concurrent performance are not due to the differential stimulus per se.

(1) differential discriminative stimuli can have stimulus effects that are not mediated by the discriminative stimuli' s effects on reinforcement distribution, and (2) these effects are more pronounced in the transition to a new condition than in final performance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how behavior changes over the course of training.
the development and application of a new approach to the study of concurrent behavior.
the development of a theoretical framework for the analysis of concurrent performance in transition, and with the empirical study of this framework.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the effects of the stimulus on concurrent performance in a transition are the same as the effects of the reinforcement distribution on performance in a transition.
the results of this experiment are consistent with the view that stimulus control is a product of the history of reinforcement and that it is a property of the organism rather than the environment.
, in general, differential stimuli do affect concurrent performance in transition, but the effects may be more subtle than those observed in final performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
stimulus control is a necessary but not sufficient condition for differential performance.

differential discriminative stimuli are not necessary to produce differential responding, but they may facilitate differential responding during the transition from non-differential to differential behavior.
stimulus control and reinforcement distribution are not independent variables in concurrent performance.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we should not expect to understand behavior in the absence of a complete history of training.
we need to be very careful in our interpretation of results when we compare the performance of nonhuman and human participants.
the effects of stimulus change on concurrent performance are not limited to the early stages of training.
